meta.title: The Night Shift Study — St Brennan's Hospital, board readout 2026
meta.description: Research readout for the hospital board: a 14-month study of 212 night nurses on 3 wards found that an earlier 06:30 handover and a 20-minute protected rest cut night-shift medication errors by 37%. Findings, limits, ranked recommendations and one funding decision.

slides.eyebrow: St Brennan's Hospital · The Night Shift Study · Board readout, November 2026
slides.heading: Rested night nurses made 37% fewer medication errors.
slides.lead: Fourteen months, three wards, 212 nurses, and one decision for the board.
slides.notes: Say the ask up front: we want funding for rest rooms on nine more wards. The rest of the deck is the evidence.

slides.heading: Two cheap changes cut night-shift medication errors by 37%

cards.title: Handover moved to 06:30
cards.body: Nurses hand over before the hour when most errors happened.

cards.title: 20 minutes of protected rest
cards.body: Taken on 81% of shifts, covered by a float nurse.

cards.title: Errors fell from 4.1 to 2.6
cards.body: Per 1,000 night doses; comparison wards fell 5%.

slides.notes: If the board reads one slide, it is this one.

slides.heading: Most night errors happened in the two hours before handover
slides.lead: Errors climbed through the night and peaked after 05:00, when nurses had been awake longest.
slides.imageAlt: Bar chart of night-shift medication errors by hour from 19:00 to 07:00, rising slowly then peaking at 05:00 and 06:00, with the new 06:30 handover and a 20-minute rest band at 03:00 marked

slides.heading: 212 nurses on three wards, compared with three wards unchanged

Night-shift doses checked by pharmacy audit

slides.heading: What we found
slides.lead: Three findings, each with its evidence.

slides.heading: Pilot-ward errors fell 37% while comparison wards barely moved
slides.lead: Errors per 1,000 night doses. Source: pharmacy audit, n = 153,000 pilot doses. Ten-month average: 2.6 vs 3.8.
slides.notes: The pilot line drops in the first quarter and keeps falling. That rules out a one-off burst of attention.

slides.quote: At half five I used to read a chart three times. Now I'm handing over before that fog comes in.
slides.by: Staff nurse, Ward 7 surgical · 11 years on nights

slides.heading: The last two hours of the night gave the biggest fall
Late and missed doses fell most; wrong-patient errors barely moved
slides.lead: Change in each error type on pilot wards, baseline vs the 10 changed months.

slides.heading: Day staff welcomed the 06:30 start, and call bells waited no longer
slides.left:
Day nurses would resist starting 30 minutes earlier.
Rest breaks would leave the ward short and slow call bells.
slides.right:
78% of day nurses preferred 06:30; it beats the rush hour.
Median call-bell wait stayed at 2.1 minutes, against 2.0 before.

slides.heading: What it means for the hospital
slides.lead: How far to trust it, and what to fund.

slides.heading: The effect is clear on general wards and untested in intensive care
rows: Wards chose to join; not randomised
No evidence for ICU or A&E
One winter in the changed period

slides.heading: Rest rooms plus the 06:30 handover would prevent about 590 errors a year
slides.lead: Options for 9 more wards, ranked by night-shift medication errors avoided per year, from pilot rates.
slides.notes: Option 3 is weak because, without a room, nurses took their rest on only 54% of shifts in the first month. A float nurse per three wards covers the break; that cost is already in the ward budget.

slides.heading: Fund rest rooms on nine wards and cut night errors by a third.
slides.lead: £540,000 once, £60,000 per ward. Rested nurses give safer doses.
